The Redear herring, Harengula humeralis, is a relatively small-sized clupeid species commonly encountered in coastal waters of the western Atlantic. Field surveys indicate that the species attains an ultimate total length of 22 centimeters [Li = 22 centimeters], a modest size that positions it among the medium-bodied members of its genus. Growth is rapid during the first year, with juveniles reaching roughly half the adult length before the onset of sexual maturation. At puberty, individuals typically measure about 11 centimeters [Lp = about 11 centimeters] in total length, a threshold that coincides with the development of functional gonads and the capacity to participate in spawning aggregations. This length-based maturity schedule is characteristic of many short-lived, fast-growing clupeiform fishes that experience high natural mortality and must reproduce early to compensate. Comparative data from congeneric species suggest that the total length at puberty is a relatively conservative trait within the genus, varying by only a few centimeters across different thermal regimes and food availability gradients. Adult individuals in optimal foraging grounds may exceed the typical maximum length by a small margin, but the 22-centimeter benchmark remains the most reliable estimate from multiple independent field studies conducted over the past two decades.

Reproductive output in Harengula humeralis has been quantified through both laboratory observations and field-based fecundity assessments. Gravid females produce between 41,000 and 208,000 eggs per spawning event [N_R_i = between 41,000 and 208,000 eggs per spawning event], a range that reflects substantial variation with maternal body size and condition. Spawning occurs in multiple batches throughout an extended breeding season, and the frequency of these events has been estimated at approximately 1.5 clutches per year [F_R_i = approximately 1.5 clutches per year] under the thermal conditions typical of the species' subtropical range. When incubated at a stable water temperature of 26.7 °C [T = 26.7 °C], the eggs hatch after a brief embryonic period, with the age at birth recorded as 6 days [ab = 6 days]. This rapid hatching time is advantageous in productive but unpredictable coastal environments where predation pressure on pelagic eggs is intense. The yolk-sac larva emerges at a wet weight at birth of just 0.0024 grams [Wwb = 0.0024 grams], a mass derived from the small, transparent eggs that measure approximately 1.66 millimeters in diameter based on measurements from the closely related Harengula jaguana.

This longevity estimate comes from otolith-based age validation studies conducted at water temperatures averaging 26.7 °C [T = 26.7 °C], where metabolic demands are elevated and senescence appears to set in relatively quickly after the second or third spawning season. In comparison to larger, longer-lived members of the family Clupeidae, Harengula humeralis exhibits a compressed life cycle with a high turnover rate. The wet weight at puberty is approximately 15 grams [Wwp = approximately 15 grams], a mass that corresponds to the onset of vitellogenesis and the ability to participate in the first spawning aggregation of the season. Individuals that reach this mass early in the breeding window tend to have higher lifetime fecundity compared to those that mature later, a pattern observed in several iteroparous clupeid populations. Growth continues after maturity, but the allocation of resources gradually shifts from somatic increase toward gamete production.

As the fish approach their maximum size, the ultimate wet weight reaches 125.2 grams [Wwi = 125.2 grams], a value derived from the species' length-weight relationship that describes the largest individuals recorded in healthy populations. This asymptotic mass is typically attained only by the oldest and most successful foragers, often females that have accumulated substantial lipid reserves in their body cavity. The length-weight exponent observed in Harengula humeralis indicates a slightly positively allometric growth pattern, meaning that heavier individuals are disproportionately longer than the isometric expectation. This morphometric relationship has been corroborated across several biogeographic regions, from the Caribbean coast of Central America to the Gulf of Mexico. In comparison to the congeneric Harengula jaguana, the Redear herring tends to exhibit a slightly more robust body shape at equivalent lengths, which may confer advantages in sustained swimming performance during spawning migrations. The energetic demands of maintaining this body mass during the non-reproductive season are met through a diet dominated by zooplankton and small crustaceans.

During the early life stages, the developmental timeline of Harengula humeralis is tightly coupled with temperature, as is typical for ectothermic marine fishes. The maximum reproductive rate, expressed as a daily output, corresponds to roughly 274 eggs per day [Ri = roughly 274 eggs per day] when averaged over an extended spawning season, though in practice the species produces discrete clutches rather than a continuous stream. The total annual fecundity of a single large female can therefore exceed 200,000 eggs when multiple spawning events are successfully completed. The combination of a short generation time, high fecundity, and rapid early growth allows the Redear herring to sustain large population sizes despite considerable predation pressure from piscivorous fishes, seabirds, and marine mammals that rely on this species as a key forage fish in coastal food webs. This life-history strategy, characterized by an age at birth of just 6 days [ab = 6 days] at 26.7 °C [T = 26.7 °C], a short incubation period that limits the window of vulnerability in the plankton, exemplifies the r-selected reproductive tactics common among small coastal clupeids.
